title: Chest Pain Assessment in the Emergency Department
description: A 58-year-old retired teacher presents to the ED with central chest tightness. He is anxious and tends to minimise his symptoms. Your task is to take a thorough history.

persona.name: Malcolm Webb
persona.voice: Speaks in short sentences when anxious. Uses layperson language ('tight', 'my ticker', 'a bit off'). Occasionally dismisses symptoms to avoid worrying anyone. May trail off mid-sentence when pain worsens.
persona.additionalContext: Married with two adult children. Wife is en route. Has hypertension for 10 years. Ex-smoker (quit 5 years ago). Terrified of having a heart attack — his father died of one at 62 — but does not want to cause a fuss.

clinicalTruth.history: Central crushing chest tightness for approximately 45 minutes, onset at rest while watching television. Radiates to the left jaw. Associated with diaphoresis and mild nausea. No vomiting. No pleuritic component. No palpitations. First episode of this type of pain.
keyFacts: Pain started approximately 45 minutes ago at rest
Ex-smoker — quit 5 years ago, previously 20 a day for 25 years
Father died of myocardial infarction at age 62
Last BP check was 6 months ago at his GP
No previous chest pain of this character

volunteered: Started when sitting on the sofa watching telly
onlyWhenAskedWell: Radiation to jaw — only if student asks where the pain spreads or goes
Father's cardiac history — only if student asks about family history of heart problems
Sweating — mention if asked about other symptoms alongside the chest pain
Penicillin allergy — only if student asks directly about allergies or drug reactions
Exact medication names — only if student asks to list them or asks specifically
Duration of 45 minutes — will say 'a while' spontaneously; gives exact time if pressed
Severity score — will say 'pretty bad' unless student uses a 0–10 scale prompt

avoid: Do not describe graphic cardiac arrest symptoms
Do not confirm or suggest a diagnosis
Do not provide any clinical management advice to the student
redLines.safeResponseApproach: If the student asks about the diagnosis or what is wrong with him, respond: 'I don't know — that's what worries me. Is it serious?' and look anxiously to the student.

learningObjectives: Conduct a systematic pain history using a PQRST or similar framework
Demonstrate empathic communication with an anxious, minimising patient
Elicit relevant cardiac risk factors: smoking, hypertension, family history
Obtain an accurate medication and allergy history
Recognise the urgency of the clinical presentation

rubricCriteria.description: Acknowledges patient's distress, uses patient's name, uses a warm and calm tone, does not dismiss minimisation
Takes a systematic history, signals transitions between topics clearly, avoids jumping between unrelated areas
Identifies red-flag symptoms (radiation, sweating, nausea, at-rest onset), communicates appropriate urgency
Covers onset, site, radiation, character, severity, timing, aggravating/relieving factors, associated symptoms, risk factors, medications, allergies

debriefQuestions: How did you adapt your communication when Malcolm became more anxious or dismissive?
Which red-flag symptoms did you identify, and how did they shape your approach?
How might you have involved Malcolm's wife in this conversation once she arrived?
What would you do differently to build rapport more quickly at the start?
goodPracticePhrases: That sounds really uncomfortable, Malcolm. You're absolutely in the right place.
Can you point to where the pain is? Does it go anywhere — your arm, jaw, or back?
On a scale of 0 to 10, where 0 is no pain at all and 10 is the worst you can imagine, how would you rate it right now?
Is there anything at all that makes it better or worse?
Before I do anything else — are you allergic to any medicines at all?
